title: Tactical vision mastery challenge
objectives: Apply the CCT habit, hanging-piece checks, forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks, and back-rank awareness across a mixed set of fresh positions

steps.text: Let's put the whole unit together. This challenge draws on every pattern from Tactical Vision — checks, captures, threats, hanging pieces, forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks, back-rank tactics, and zwischenzug — on fresh positions you haven't seen before. Take your time on each one.

steps.prompt: Nothing looks urgent — scan for check anyway, and play it.

hints.text: Run the CCT check: is there a check available even though nothing is under attack?
Your rook's file lines up with the king's rank if it slides all the way up.
Slide the rook here.
Ra8 delivers check — always run the CCT scan, even in a quiet-looking position.

feedback.default: That doesn't give check. Look for a rook move along a rank or file that lines up with the king.

steps.successExplanation: Ra8+ delivers check — the CCT habit in action, even with nothing else happening on the board.

hints.text: Check the whole diagonal, not just the nearby squares — is the knight actually defended by anything?
Nothing defends the knight.
Capture here.
Qxd5 wins the knight for free — always check the exact geometry before assuming a piece is safe.

feedback.default: That doesn't win the knight. Check whether anything actually defends d5 before deciding it's safe.

steps.successExplanation: Qxd5 wins the knight for free — nothing defended it.

steps.prompt: Move the knight to fork the king and the rook.

hints.text: Look for a square where your knight would attack both the king and the rook at once.
These are the two pieces to fork.
Jump here.
Ne4+ forks the king and the rook — the rook falls next move.

feedback.default: That's a legal knight move, but it doesn't attack both the king and the rook. Look for the square where the knight's L-shape lines up with both pieces at once.

steps.successExplanation: Ne4+ forks the king on g5 (check!) and the rook on c5 at the same time — the rook falls next move.

steps.prompt: The rook on c5 is pinned and can't recapture without exposing the king. Capture the pawn it's 'defending.'

hints.text: The rook can't move off the c-file without exposing its own king — so does it really defend the pawn next to it?
Your bishop's diagonal reaches the pawn directly.
Capture here.
Bxd5 wins the pawn for free. The rook on c5 is pinned to its own king along the c-file and can't legally recapture.

feedback.default: That doesn't win the pawn cleanly. Check whether the pinned rook can actually recapture here.

steps.successExplanation: Bxd5 wins the pawn. A rook absolutely pinned to its king can't defend anything off its own file.

steps.prompt: Move the rook onto the file where it skewers the king and wins the rook behind it.

hints.text: The king and the enemy rook already share a file. Get your rook onto that same file.
The king and rook are both on this file.
Slide here.
Rb1+ skewers the king and the rook behind it — the king must move, and the rook falls.

feedback.default: That doesn't create a skewer. Find the file the king and the enemy rook already share.

steps.successExplanation: Rb1+ skewers the king and the rook on b8. Once the king moves off the file, the rook is yours.

steps.prompt: Move the knight to capture the bishop — notice what your rook can suddenly see once the knight is out of the way.

hints.text: Your knight is blocking your rook's view down the d-file. What's on that file, behind the knight?
The bishop is undefended and reachable in one jump.
Capture here.
Nxc6 wins the bishop, and moving the knight uncovers a discovered attack on the rook on d8 from your own rook.

feedback.default: That doesn't win the bishop. Find the knight's capture, then notice what opens up behind it.

steps.successExplanation: Nxc6 wins the bishop, and clears the d-file for a discovered attack on the rook on d8 — two gains from one move.

steps.prompt: A king castled behind three unmoved pawns is always completely safe from back-rank tactics.

feedback.default: It can still be mated along the back rank if it has no escape square while a rook or queen infiltrates — the very pawns that shield it also block its own escape. That's exactly why creating luft matters.

steps.successExplanation: Right — pawns in front of the king don't guarantee safety; they can trap it just as easily as protect it.

steps.prompt: Your knight can recapture on e5 any time — it's not going anywhere. Grab the undefended rook first.

hints.text: The knight on e5 isn't defended and isn't running away — no need to recapture it this instant.
The rook is undefended and reachable right now.
Capture here.
Bxg5 wins the rook — the zwischenzug idea: grab the more valuable, undefended piece before finishing the 'expected' recapture.

feedback.default: That doesn't win the rook. The knight on e5 can wait — look for the undefended piece you can win right now.

steps.successExplanation: Bxg5 wins the rook. The recapture on e5 was never going anywhere, so there was no rush to play it first.

steps.summary: You've now applied every pattern from Tactical Vision on fresh positions: scanning for checks, captures, and threats before anything else; spotting hanging pieces mid-combination; forks from every piece; pins and the false defense they create; skewers; discovered attacks; back-rank danger in both directions; and zwischenzug's in-between moves. These patterns don't retire once you've learned them — real games combine them constantly, and recognizing them quickly is what turns calculation from slow and effortful into fast and automatic.
